source: Wikipedia (2026 fetch) CLARION (cognitive architecture)
finding: CLARION has four subsystems: action-centered (ACS), non-action-centered (NACS), motivational, meta-cognitive. Each has two levels: a top explicit level (localist chunk nodes and rules) and a bottom implicit level (distributed micro-feature nodes in neural networks). Chunks link the two levels.
numbers: No numbers. Implicit learning is Q-learning; explicit learning is one-shot hypothesis testing; bottom-up learning uses the Rule-Extraction-Refinement (RER) algorithm.
limits: Encyclopedia summary, not primary. Implicit/explicit is kept separate from procedural/declarative.
agent_relevance: Names the exact hybrid pattern: a neural/intuitive layer plus a symbolic rule layer with learned links both ways. Our scaffold has a program layer and a model layer; CLARION says model output can be turned into rules (bottom-up) and rules can prompt the model (top-down).

source: Sun, Slusarz, Terry (2005) The interaction of the explicit and the implicit in skill learning: a dual-process approach. Psychological Review 112(1):159-192 (PubMed abstract)
finding: Argues that implicit and explicit skill learning interact and give synergy effects, and that learning should be bottom-up (implicit first, then explicit). CLARION is used to simulate a range of quantitative human data.
numbers: Abstract only; no figures read. Full text was not reachable (publisher paywalled, author site moved).
limits: Only abstract read. Exact task-by-task fits not verified this session.
agent_relevance: Core claim for hybrids: combining the two kinds of knowledge beats either alone. Needs an LLM test: does prompting with extracted rules plus raw intuition beat either one?

source: Wikipedia CLARION: list of simulated tasks
finding: CLARION has been used on the serial reaction time task, artificial grammar learning, process control, a categorical inference task, alphabetic arithmetic, Tower of Hanoi, and a minefield navigation task. SRT and process control are mostly implicit; Hanoi and alphabetic arithmetic have much explicit processing.
numbers: Six tasks plus minefield navigation; no fit statistics given.
limits: List only. No effect sizes.
agent_relevance: Shows the test bed. Tasks where verbalisation hurts (process control, SRT) are where our rule to force explicit checks is most at risk.

source: Domangue, Mathews, Sun, Roussel, Guidry (2004) Effects of model-based and memory-based processing on speed and accuracy of grammar string generation. JEP:LMC 30(5):1002-1011 (PubMed abstract)
finding: Three experiments on an artificial grammar. Model-based training (conscious mental model) gave slow but accurate responses. Memory-based training (instances) gave fast, less accurate responses. People prefer the memory-based mode when both are trained. Accuracy from model-based training faded over a retention interval.
numbers: 3 experiments; N not in abstract.
limits: Abstract only. Cited by Sun as support for the two-system split.
agent_relevance: A speed-accuracy split matches fast intuition versus slow explicit reasoning. Suggests a budget rule: use the cheap path unless exactness is required, and expect explicit rule gains to decay if not refreshed.

source: Wilson, Sun, Mathews (2009) A motivationally-based simulation of performance degradation under pressure. Neural Networks 22(5-6):502-508 (PubMed abstract)
finding: CLARION gives a mechanistic account of choking under pressure that combines motivation with the balance of implicit and explicit processes. It is offered to unite the distraction theory and the explicit-monitoring theory.
numbers: No figures in abstract.
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Mechanism for 'overthinking hurts': too much weight on the explicit level degrades well-practised skill. Supports keeping explicit checks off where plain output is already reliable (links to G1).

source: Helie & Sun (2010) Incubation, insight, and creative problem solving: a unified theory and a connectionist model. Psychological Review 117(3):994-1024
finding: Explicit-Implicit Interaction (EII) theory has five principles: explicit and implicit knowledge coexist and differ; both run in most tasks; knowledge is redundantly coded; results are integrated; processing iterates, possibly in both directions. Implemented in CLARION's NACS.
numbers: Four human data sets simulated: Yaniv and Meyer 1987 lexical decision priming, Smith and Vela 1991 reminiscence, Durso et al. 1994 insight graphs, Schooler et al. 1993 overshadowing.
limits: Model has many free parameters (Tables 4-5). Authors say EII cannot cover all incubation cases.
agent_relevance: A concrete loop: implicit settle, send up to explicit, integrate, check confidence against a threshold, if low run an abductive step and iterate. Maps to a program loop around an LLM with a confidence threshold, bounded by a time limit.

source: Helie & Sun (2010) model mechanics
finding: Bottom level is a bidirectional associative network (NDRAM) that settles. Each settling step is a 'spin' timed at about 350 ms. The result goes bottom-up (explicitation), is integrated with rule results, turned into a Boltzmann distribution, and the mode sets an internal confidence level (ICL). If ICL is under a threshold the answer is sent back down for another round.
numbers: 350 ms per spin; participants had 2 s in lexical decision = 6 spins; free recall 42 spins; one run of 20,571 spins is about 2 hours.
limits: Time mapping is a modelling assumption taken from Sun and Zhang 2004.
agent_relevance: Gives a template for a confidence gate: output only when the top option clears a threshold, otherwise re-query. Noise (temperature) is the creativity knob.

source: Helie & Sun (2010) Simulation: Yaniv and Meyer 1987 lexical decision priming
finding: After a failed rare-word association, words related to the unsolved target are recognised faster (priming), but only when the person rated feeling-of-knowing high. The model reproduced this.
numbers: Model: target faster than distractor after a correct response, t(2976)=6.87, p<.0001; after an incorrect response t(2221)=1.91, ns. Human: t(2100)=8.5, p<.001 for the correct-response difference; incorrect-response difference t(2100)=0.7, ns. Several thousand simulated participants.
limits: Very high power from thousands of simulated runs; the human original used far fewer people.
agent_relevance: Implicit memory carries traces of unsolved problems. Analogue: keep failed attempts in context as primes, not only as errors.

source: Helie & Sun (2010) Simulation: Smith and Vela 1991 reminiscence in free recall
finding: Recall in a second test rises with incubation interval. The model reproduced the increase.
numbers: Human: incubation interval effect F(3,209)=9.40, p<.01; mean reminiscence 2.90, 3.15, 3.72, 5.00 for 0, 1, 5, 10 min; test duration F(2,209)=0.27, ns. Simulated interval effect F(3,11998) significant.
limits: The paper models only one data set; reminiscence has had mixed results elsewhere.
agent_relevance: Incubation gain is time-linked, not effort-linked. For a stateless LLM a pause does nothing unless sampling or re-prompting supplies the 'spins'.

source: Helie & Sun (2010) Simulation: Durso, Rea, Dayton 1994 insight graphs; noise and solving
finding: Solving an insight riddle needs a new explicit representation. In the model, solving probability rose with noise (temperature) at low noise and then levelled off.
numbers: 8 noise levels, 1000 runs each; effect of noise on edge distance F(7,7992)=12,193.40, p<.0001; each step from 10^-2 to 10^0 helped at p<.01, beyond that no gain.
limits: Durso et al. gave no statistics, so no formal comparison with humans.
agent_relevance: Supports a temperature sweep on stuck problems with a saturation point. Do not keep raising it.

source: Helie & Sun (2010) Simulation: Schooler, Ohlsson, Brooks 1993 verbal overshadowing in insight
finding: Humans who verbalised their strategy during an interruption solved fewer insight problems than those doing an unrelated task. CLARION reproduced the drop by letting verbal explicit processing dominate.
numbers: Human (Schooler 1993 Exp 1): 45.8% unrelated vs 35.6% verbalise, t(74)=2.13, p<.05, about 30% relative drop. Model, 5000 runs per condition: 45.3% vs 35.3%.
limits: Model fits one study. The 2010 paper does not discuss later mixed replications of verbal overshadowing.
agent_relevance: Strongest boundary condition for explain-your-steps operators: forced verbalisation can lower performance on insight-type problems, in the model only when rules are ineffective for the problem.

source: Helie & Sun (2010) Principle 1 and bottom-up learning evidence review
finding: Cites that implicit skill improves before verbal knowledge in dynamic control tasks (Stanley et al. 1989), artificial grammar (Reber and Lewis 1977) and minefield navigation (Sun et al. 2001): the delay suggests explicit knowledge is extracted from implicit skill (bottom-up learning). The opposite direction, top-down assimilation, shows in automaticity such as alphabetic arithmetic moving from counting to memory retrieval.
numbers: No new numbers; secondary citations only.
limits: Review inside a modelling paper, author-favourable. Competing account in the PMC9177494 line below.
agent_relevance: Bottom-up: mine rules from successful traces. Top-down: compile stable rules into cheap fast calls, as SwiftSage does.

source: Laird, Lebiere, Rosenbloom (2017) A Standard Model of the Mind. AI Magazine
finding: Consensus across ACT-R, Soar and Sigma. It breaks with the pure symbolic tradition: computation at the deliberate-act level is hybrid, with symbols plus quantitative metadata (frequency, recency, utility, activation) and statistical learning (Bayesian and reinforcement). Parallel inside modules, with a serial bottleneck. CLARION and Sigma are named as having both symbolic and distributed forms.
numbers: About 50 ms cognitive cycle. No experimental numbers.
quote: the standard model involves a hybrid combination of symbolic and statistical processing
limits: Consensus of three chosen architectures; CLARION was not one of them. Strict rule: relations cannot be defined over the numeric metadata.
agent_relevance: The field's agreed minimum: symbols for structure, numbers only as annotations. For us: keep final decisions on symbolic, checkable objects; use model scores only as metadata.

source: Laird, Lebiere, Rosenbloom (2017) Standard Model: what architectures claim to cover
finding: Psychology-focused architectures (ACT-R, Clarion, LIDA) fit data from controlled experiments. AI-focused ones (Soar, Sigma) develop functional capability. Neuro ones (Leabra, Spaun) use brain-like mechanisms for simple tasks.
numbers: None.
limits: Descriptive.
agent_relevance: CLARION is validated on human data, Sigma on function. For an LLM agent, human-data validation is a weak guide and benchmarks are the real test.

source: Rosenbloom, Demski, Ustun (2016) The Sigma cognitive architecture and system: towards functionally elegant grand unification. J. Artificial General Intelligence 7(1):1-103
finding: Sigma rests on a graphical architecture hypothesis: factor graphs with summary-product message passing give one mechanism for symbols, probabilities and neural-style learning. Four desiderata: grand unification, generic cognition, functional elegance, sufficient efficiency. Mixed (symbolic plus probabilistic) and hybrid (discrete plus continuous) representations are native.
numbers: Target cycle about 50 ms; simple tasks run within 50 ms, virtual humans about 250 ms per cycle.
limits: Qualitative evaluation against its own desiderata. No head-to-head benchmark against other architectures.
agent_relevance: Opposite design to CLARION: one uniform substrate, not two separate levels. Warns that unification costs speed. Our scaffold is closer to the two-level design.

source: Rosenbloom et al. (2016) Sigma learning: gradient descent in every function
finding: One learning rule, gradient descent over factor functions, gives concept learning, clustering, HMM perception, action models and reinforcement learning as idioms. Supervised concepts were tested on word-sense and tagging tasks.
numbers: Word sense disambiguation 78% (Senseval-3) and 70.3% (Semcor). Part-of-speech tagging 90.3%, no better than the most-common-tag baseline. Isolated word recognition 99.2% on 10 digits (chance 10%).
limits: Own benchmarks; POS result only matches a trivial baseline. Sigma lags specialist NLP systems.
agent_relevance: A unified architecture reaches baseline level, not state of the art. Do not expect an architecture alone to lift accuracy; gain must come from control logic.

source: Rosenbloom et al. (2016) Sigma efficiency findings
finding: Cost depends on treewidth and the number of distinct nonzero regions in functions. Message ordering matters.
numbers: Speedup factor of about 100 with 100 words and about 1000 with 1000 words in a vocabulary-sized graph (one optimisation); 15-20% faster on loopy Nash-equilibrium graphs with loop-depth ordering.
limits: Single-thread serial message passing. Learning adds regions each cycle and raises cost.
agent_relevance: Analogy for token cost: unified deliberation scales badly with problem size, which favours cheap gating as in SwiftSage.

source: Rosenbloom (2013) The Sigma cognitive architecture and system. AISB Quarterly (preprint)
finding: Short overview of Sigma. The cognitive cycle maps onto the 50 ms human cycle with perception, graph-solution (memory access) and graph-modification phases. Gradient-descent learning is inspired by local learning in Bayesian networks that matched backpropagation without a separate backward pass.
numbers: 50 ms cycle target.
limits: Overview; no new experiments.
agent_relevance: Background only.

source: Stocco, Laird, Lebiere, Rosenbloom (2018) Empirical evidence from neuroimaging data for a Standard Model of the Mind. CogSci
finding: Dynamic causal modelling on fMRI from four tasks (Flanker, Stroop, Raven matrices, rapid instructed task learning). The Standard Model connectivity beat a structural-only and a fully connected alternative in every dataset.
numbers: Combined N=103 (datasets of 26, 28, 24, 25 analysed). Posterior probability of SMM being best at least 0.99. Log-likelihood advantage d > 124 vs the structural model and d >= 30 vs the fully connected model; d > 30 counted as strong evidence.
limits: Only two alternatives tested; four cognitive-control and reasoning tasks; no memory, language or decision tasks; authors call it preliminary. The rank of the two alternatives changed between tasks.
agent_relevance: Weak neural support for the hybrid-architecture skeleton. It says nothing about whether a scaffold helps an LLM.

source: Rosenbloom (2017) Lessons from mapping Sigma onto the Standard Model of the Mind. AAAI Fall Symposium
finding: Three open issues for the Standard Model from the Sigma mapping: self-monitoring, memory and learning, and symbols. Sigma's hybrid nature and tensor/vector view blur the symbol boundary: symbols may be substructure-free or patterns over vectors.
numbers: None.
limits: Position paper.
agent_relevance: The symbol-versus-vector line is soft even inside architectures. Our program/model split is a design choice, not a natural kind.

source: Laird, Lebiere, Rosenbloom, Stocco (2025) A proposal to extend the Common Model of Cognition with metacognition. arXiv 2506.07807
finding: Contrasts a hierarchical metacognition design (specialised modules on top of cognition, as in MIDCA and CLARION) with a unified design where metacognition is ordinary reasoning over cognition facts placed in working memory. Proposes the unified one with minimal architectural change.
numbers: None; proposal.
limits: Only the introduction was read in detail. No experiments.
agent_relevance: CLARION's separate metacognitive subsystem is the 'on top' pattern. Our program-as-controller is also 'on top'. Their alternative is to let the model reason about its own trace.

source: Rosenbloom (2025) A qualitative comparative evaluation of cognitive and generative theories. Advances in Cognitive Systems
finding: Compares symbolic and hybrid cognitive architectures with LLM-based generative architectures on fidelity, lawfulness, usability, beauty and comprehensiveness. Generative theories win on lawfulness and usability of the architecture itself and on shared benchmarks. Cognitive theories win on the variable content (knowledge) they process. Neither is beautiful yet.
numbers: Qualitative; no measurements.
quote: neither type of theory is able to yield truly beautiful systems at this point
limits: Author's own framework, no numbers.
agent_relevance: Frames our task: the LLM gives breadth and ease, a cognitive scaffold gives control and inspectable content.

source: Sun (2024) Can a cognitive architecture fundamentally enhance LLMs? Or vice versa? arXiv 2401.10444
finding: Position paper: LLMs roughly capture implicit processes (intuition and instinct). Explicit symbolic processes plus motivation, memory and metacognition are missing. Proposes LLMs as the bottom level of CLARION. Top-down activation becomes prompts to the LLM; bottom-up activation becomes LLM outputs mapped to chunks and rules. The explicit level prompts, verifies, refines, explains or overrides LLM results.
numbers: No experiments and no measurements.
limits: Untested claim, author-motivated. Argues interaction is bidirectional, unlike the default-intervention view of Evans and Frankish.
agent_relevance: Closest statement of our design from the CLARION side. It gives the testable prediction: explicit rules that verify or override LLM output beat both alone. No data yet.

source: Sun (2024) Five roles for LLMs in CLARION and the reasoning claim
finding: Lists five ways to put LLMs in CLARION (perception, language, action specification, implicit memory, or all implicit roles) and prefers the last. Says search control (depth-first, breadth-first, A*) can be run by explicit processes through repeated prompts, and cites reasoning templates that raise LLM reasoning (Xie et al. 2023).
numbers: None.
limits: Design discussion only.
agent_relevance: Supports program-driven search with the model as node expander or scorer.

source: Lin et al. (2023) SwiftSage: a generative agent with fast and slow thinking for complex interactive tasks. NeurIPS
finding: Dual-process LLM agent. SWIFT is a small fine-tuned T5 (770M) imitating oracle trajectories; SAGE prompts GPT-4 for subgoal planning and grounding when needed. A fixed heuristic switches to SAGE on: five steps of zero reward, an invalid predicted action, a critical decision, or an unexpected observation.
numbers: ScienceWorld, 30 task types: SwiftSage 84.68 average score vs Reflexion 45.34, ReAct 36.43, SayCan 33.82, DRRN 15.56. Tokens per action: SwiftSage 757.07 vs SayCan 1855.84, ReAct 1971.03, Reflexion 2983.46. With GPT-3.5 instead of GPT-4: SwiftSage 62.22; ReAct 36.43 down to 19.76.
limits: Fast module needs oracle trajectories (offline imitation). One benchmark. Switch rule is hand-coded; authors suggest learning it. Small ablation of planning questions only.
agent_relevance: Best direct LLM test of the hybrid fast/slow idea with measured gain. The switch triggers are program-checked signals, matching G1. The fast path is trained, which our no-training rule forbids, but a cached-answer path could play that role.

source: Pan, Albalak, Wang, Wang (2023) Logic-LM: empowering LLMs with symbolic solvers for faithful logical reasoning. EMNLP Findings
finding: The LLM translates a problem into symbolic form, a deterministic solver (Prover9, Z3, python-constraint, Pyke) reasons, and solver errors drive self-refinement. A neuro-symbolic hybrid with the LLM as translator.
numbers: Five datasets. GPT-4 standard/CoT/Logic-LM: ProofWriter 52.67/68.11/79.66; FOLIO 69.11/70.58/78.92; LogicalDeduction 71.33/75.25/87.63; AR-LSAT 33.33/35.06/43.04; PrOntoQA 77.40/98.79/83.20. ChatGPT average gain 39.2% over standard and 18.4% over CoT. Self-refinement raised executable rate, e.g. FOLIO 66.7% to 84.3% with ChatGPT.
limits: Logic-LM lost to CoT on PrOntoQA with GPT-4 (83.20 vs 98.79). Gains depend on translation succeeding: AR-LSAT executable rate only 11.3% before refinement with ChatGPT. Logic problems only.
agent_relevance: The explicit symbolic layer helps most where reasoning is non-linear (FOL, constraints) and can hurt where forward chaining already works. Supports G2: revise from real solver output.

source: Sumers, Yao, Narasimhan, Griffiths (2024) Cognitive architectures for language agents (CoALA). TMLR
finding: Framework that organises language agents by memory, action space and decision cycle, linked to Soar and ACT-R. Cited by Sun 2024 as a survey of this direction.
numbers: Not read this session; only the title page was extracted.
limits: Not opened beyond the title page. Covered in sibling subfield 10.
agent_relevance: Pointer only.

source: What triggers explicit awareness in implicit sequence learning? Implications from theories of consciousness (2022, PMC9177494)
finding: Competing account of how explicit knowledge arises from implicit learning. The Unexpected Event Hypothesis says conscious knowledge appears when an unexpected event triggers attention and top-down amplification, in line with Global Workspace and higher-order theories. It argues gradual bottom-up strengthening is unlikely to win access to the workspace alone.
numbers: Review; no new effect sizes in the parts read.
limits: Skimmed the abstract, introduction and parts of the discussion. Concerns serial reaction time and artificial grammar tasks.
agent_relevance: Challenges CLARION's smooth bottom-up extraction: explicit rule discovery may need a surprise signal. That matches our rule to revise only when a check fails.

source: Helie & Sun (2010) overshadowing robustness and explicit search in implicit tasks
finding: Implicit learning work (Berry and Broadbent 1988; Reber 1989) shows that looking for rules can hurt when none exist or they are hard to find. This overshadowing is described as robust and is a boundary condition for explicit hypothesis search.
numbers: None given in the section read.
limits: Secondary claim; no replications cited.
agent_relevance: Do not force rule-hunting on tasks where earlier attempts show no stable rule (random or noisy items).

source: Rosenbloom site publications list (2026)
finding: Rosenbloom's page lists Sigma and Standard Model work through 2025, including three 2025 arXiv papers (2412.16231, 2506.07807, 2506.12224) and an MIT Press open-access monograph 'On Minds'. No LLM-in-Sigma benchmark paper is listed.
numbers: None.
limits: Index only.
agent_relevance: Sigma has not been combined with an LLM with measurements on this list; the hybrid-with-LLM evidence comes from other groups.
